units.title: Panel layout
units.summary: A map of the top panel — mode keys, module keys, track and step keys, transport, keyboard, function keys, encoders, screen and sockets — and the names this manual uses for each.

facts.text: Seen from above, the controls sit on a grid of 17 columns and 6 rows. The top two rows hold the speaker, the volume knob, the screen and the four encoders; keys fill the four rows below.

Row three runs mode keys, `M1`…`M4`, then `T1`…`T8`; row four is `step 1`…`step 16`; the bottom two rows put `record`, `play`, `stop` above `[-]`, `[+]`, `shift` on the left, with the keyboard to their right.
The rightmost column holds `sample`, `com`, `player` and `bar`, top to bottom; `project` and `tempo` sit just below the volume knob.

Four keys pick the main mode: `instrument` for the eight sound tracks, `auxiliary` for the eight utility tracks (brain, punch-in FX, external gear, tape, send effects), `arrange` for patterns, scenes and songs, and `mix` for levels, pans, EQ and the master compressor.
The keys printed 1 to 4 directly under the screen are the module keys, written `M1`…`M4`. Each opens one page of the current mode, and the four encoders then edit what that page shows.
Arrange is the only main mode without module pages.
Some pages keep a second set of parameters on a shift layer, reached by holding `shift`.
The eight track keys under the encoders choose which track you edit — an instrument track in instrument mode, an auxiliary track in auxiliary mode.
The sixteen step keys across the middle form the step sequencer, the grid you program notes and sounds into.
`record` arms recording of notes and knob moves, `play` starts playback and `stop` halts it.
Pressing `play` again during playback jumps back to the start of the pattern.
A second press of `stop` cuts off every note and sound that is still ringing.
`[-]` and `[+]` move the keyboard one octave down or up; several pages give them other jobs.
`shift` does nothing alone: held with another key it opens that key's secondary function or page.
The two-octave keyboard of 24 keys lies right of the transport keys, below the step keys.
Every white key carries the icon of one step component; counted from the left they are `natural 1`…`natural 14`.
The ten black keys double as number keys, marked 1–9 and 0 from the left; this manual calls them `accidental 1`…`accidental 0`.
`sample` (top right corner) starts sampling from any screen.
`project` opens the list of projects, where you create, open and manage them.
`tempo` sets the song speed, the swing and the metronome.
`com` is the hub for system settings, wired and wireless connections and output routing.
`player` turns the notes of a track into arpeggios, chords and other note effects.
`bar` lengthens the sequence and holds sequence-wide settings such as quantisation.
The volume knob is at the top left, next to the speaker.
The four encoders shade from dark to light: dark gray, mid gray, light gray and white. This manual calls them `E1`, `E2`, `E3` and `E4` in that order.
The pitchbend strip on the lower left edge responds to pressure — push its left end to bend down, its right end to bend up.
The right side carries the power switch, the USB-C port and four 3.5 mm jacks — audio out, multi-out, MIDI in and audio in.
A small built-in microphone and a vertical LED level meter sit in the top right margin.
Holding `com` turns the level meter into a rough battery gauge.

units.body:
The OP-XY packs everything into one flat grid of square keys, so a few landmarks make it easy to
find your way. The left block is about _where you are_: the four mode keys (`instrument`,
`auxiliary`, `arrange`, `mix`) and, below them, the transport. The middle is about _what you edit_:
the module keys `M1`…`M4` under the screen choose a page, the track keys under the encoders choose a
track, and the step keys below them are the sequencer. The right-hand column holds the utility keys
(`sample`, `com`, `player`, `bar`).

Most editing follows one pattern: pick a mode, pick a track, pick a page, then turn `E1`…`E4`.
`shift` reaches a second layer of almost every key and page, and the keyboard's white and black keys
double as step-component and number keys when a page asks for them.

units.title: Parameter locks
units.summary: Store a module-page value on individual steps; whenever such a step plays, the parameter jumps to the stored value.

facts.text: To lock a value, keep a step held and turn an encoder; the step remembers the value you dial in.
Each time the sequencer reaches a locked step, the parameter takes that step's stored value.
Any parameter on the four module pages can carry locks; the settings of players cannot.
By default the value jumps at each locked step. The shape control in the bar menu (`bar + turn E4`) smooths the movement between locks.
Knob moves recorded live while holding `record` are also stored step by step, so they play back stepped until you add smoothing.
Copying a step to an empty step brings its locks along with its notes and step components.
`bar + M2` removes every lock in the pattern and leaves the notes in place.
Clearing the whole track with `record + hold stop` removes its locks too.
The skip parameter lock step component (`natural 12`) lets a step's locks play only on every Nth pass, for automation that appears once every few repeats.
Tracks using the drum or synth sampler accept locks as well.
Duplicating a bar with `bar + shift + [+]` copies its locks and step components too.
Shifting a track's sequence with `Tn + [-]/[+]` moves the locks together with the notes.
A lock can sit on a step that has no note; before OS 1.1.33 a bug prevented adding one there.

procedures.goal: Lock a parameter value on one step
preconditions: the module page with the parameter is on screen

steps.note: keep holding the step while turning; any page parameter works

procedures.result: The step plays back with the new value from now on.

procedures.goal: Record knob movements into the pattern while it plays
procedures.result: The movement is stored per step, like locks.

procedures.goal: Glide between locked values instead of jumping
Remove all locks from the pattern but keep its notes
Copy a step, locks included, to another step

steps.note: let go of the first step, then press the target step, which must be empty

units.body:
A parameter lock pins one value of one parameter to one step. Hold a hi-hat step and open the
filter a little, hold the next one and close it, and the pattern gains movement without any
recording pass. Locks work on everything the module pages show — engine, envelopes, filter, LFO —
but not on player settings.

Locks and live-recorded knob moves share their storage and their smoothing: both change the value
in steps unless the bar menu's shape control (`bar + turn E4`) blends between them. To thin locks
out over time, pair them with the skip parameter lock step component.

Firmware history matters here: sampler tracks gained locks in 1.1.0, rotating a sequence has
carried its locks along since 1.1.21, and locks on empty steps work reliably from 1.1.33.

units.title: Step components
units.summary: Per-step modifiers — repeats, ratchets, fixed velocity, pitch ramps, randomness, glides, bends, transposition, jumps and skip rules — added by holding `shift`, choosing a white key for the component and a black key for its value.

facts.text: A step component changes how a step plays — repeating it, splitting it into rapid retriggers, bending, randomising or skipping it — while the recorded notes stay as they are.
There are 14 components, one per white key; the icon printed on each natural names its component.

From the left, the naturals are: 1 pulse, 2 pulse hold, 3 multiply, 4 velocity, 5 ramp up, 6 ramp down, 7 random, 8 portamento, 9 bend, 10 tonality, 11 jump, 12 skip parameter lock, 13 skip step component, 14 skip trigger.
The black keys then pick the component's value. Each component reads the ten digits its own way, and the screen spells out what the chosen digit does.
For ten of the 14 components, `accidental 0` (the last black key) picks a random amount, count or shape; ramp up, ramp down, random and tonality use it for their strongest setting instead.
While `shift` is down, steps that hold notes turn dim to show they carry no component yet, and steps you select blink.
A single step can carry any combination of the 14 components at the same time.
To take a component off, select the same steps with `shift` held and press that component's white key again.
Pulse and pulse hold stretch time — the step repeats or holds for extra steps before the sequence moves on — whereas multiply fits several triggers inside the one step, the classic ratchet.
Duplicating a bar copies its notes together with their step components and locks.
Shifting a track's sequence with `Tn + [-]/[+]` carries the step components along with the notes.
Holding a step and changing its note no longer wipes the step's components; OS 1.1.32 fixed that.

procedures.goal: Add a step component to one or more steps
preconditions: the track already has notes in its sequence

steps.note: keep shift down throughout — select the steps, choose the component, then its value

procedures.result: Once `shift` is released, the chosen steps play with the component.

procedures.goal: Remove a step component

steps.note: select the same steps, then press the white key of the component to take off

units.body:
Step components are the OP-XY's answer to trig conditions and ratchets: small rules attached to a
step that change how it plays every time the pattern comes round. The keyboard becomes their control
surface while `shift` is held — the 14 white keys choose _which_ component, the 10 black keys choose
_how much_.

The components fall into a few families. Timing: pulse, pulse hold and multiply. Level: velocity.
Pitch: ramp up, ramp down, random, portamento, bend and tonality. Flow: jump moves the playhead to
another step. The three skip components thin things out, letting locks, components or the whole
trigger through only on some passes, which keeps long loops from sounding repetitive.

Because one step can stack several components, simple patterns grow into evolving ones quickly. The
value each digit selects is listed per component in the step-component reference.

units.title: Prism synth engine
units.summary: A general-purpose synth engine for bass lines, leads and most other parts; its M1 page covers waveform, oscillator ratio, detune and stereo width.

facts.text: Prism is one of the eight built-in synth engines. Each instrument track runs one engine, chosen per track.
Prism is the everyday workhorse among the engines, suited to bass lines, leads and most parts in between.
Only the M1 page belongs to the engine. Envelopes (M2), filter (M3) and LFO (M4) work the same whichever synth engine a track uses.
Like every module-page parameter, prism's four M1 settings can be parameter-locked per step.
Over MIDI, the four M1 encoders answer CC12, CC13, CC14 and CC15 on the track's channel, whatever engine is loaded.

procedures.goal: Put the prism engine on the selected instrument track
procedures.result: The track now plays through prism and M1 shows its four parameters.

parameters.name: detune
parameters.note: small pitch offset between the oscillators, for a thicker sound

parameters.name: stereo
parameters.note: how far the oscillators spread across the stereo field

units.body:
Prism runs several oscillators and gives you four controls over how they relate: their waveform,
their tuning ratio, how far apart they drift in pitch and how wide they spread. Little detune and a
narrow image keep it tight for bass; more of both makes it broad enough for leads and pads.

Everything else about the sound — how notes start and fade (M2), the filter (M3) and modulation
(M4) — is shared by all engines, so a prism patch is shaped the same way as any other synth patch.
TE's guide gives no numeric ranges or defaults for prism's parameters; read them off the screen
while turning, and treat the CC numbers as community findings rather than TE documentation.

units.title: Save over the same preset snapshot
units.summary: Since OS 1.1.17, holding shift while saving a track's sound overwrites the snapshot it was loaded from instead of adding a new one. TE's guide does not mention it.

facts.text: The regular save, `Tn + M4` in instrument mode, stores the track's current sound as a preset.
A regular save creates a new snapshot instead of replacing the one the sound came from.
Keeping `shift` held while you save writes the sound back into the snapshot it came from.
Press the keys in the right order. `shift + Tn` on its own opens the preset browser, where `M4` deletes the selected user preset — so hold the track key first, then add `shift`.
On OS 1.1.17, saving into the same snapshot could lose the preset's samples; 1.1.18 fixed it, so use the feature on 1.1.18 or later.
Over MTP, the unit's storage shows a presets/snapshot folder next to the folders of user sound packs.

procedures.goal: Overwrite the loaded snapshot with the track's current sound
preconditions: the track's sound was loaded from a saved snapshot

steps.note: hold the track key as for a normal save, add shift, then press M4 — the changelog only says to hold shift, so this order is not yet confirmed on a unit

procedures.result: The snapshot is updated in place; no new snapshot appears.

units.body:
Every regular save of a track's sound adds another snapshot, which is safe but fills the preset
folders with near-copies while you refine a patch. OS 1.1.17 added the alternative: hold `shift`
while saving and the snapshot you are working on is updated instead.

The guide (v1.1.15) predates the feature, so the exact gesture comes from the changelog alone.
Mind the order of the keys: starting with `shift` and then the track key opens the preset browser,
where `M4` means delete. Update to 1.1.18 or later before relying on it, because the first release
of the feature could drop the preset's samples.

units.title: MIDI settings
units.summary: The midi section of the system settings sets, separately for clock, notes and everything else, whether the OP-XY listens, transmits or does both; it also picks the channel that always plays the selected track and switches echo on or off.

facts.text: The MIDI options are one section of the system settings, reached with `com → M1`.
The section has five settings: clock, notes, other (every remaining message type), active track channel and midi echo.
Notes arriving on the active track channel play whichever track is currently selected.
On a unit with stock settings (OS 1.1.33) the section reads: clock in, notes both, other both, active track channel 1, midi echo off.
Clock, notes and other each take a direction; in (receive only) and both (receive and send) are confirmed on OS 1.1.33.
Community tools also describe out (send only) and off for these three settings.
With clock set to in, pressing `play` or `stop` sends nothing — no start, no stop, no clock ticks.

With clock set to both, every press of `play` sends a MIDI start (FA) — a press during playback sends another start — and `stop` sends a MIDI stop (FC). No continue (FB) or song position (F2) messages were seen.
With clock set to both, clock ticks (F8, 24 per quarter note) stream all the time, even while stopped.
With clock set to both, a start (FA) or stop (FC) from a computer starts or stops playback, and the unit sends the message back out.
Software that follows the OP-XY's play state and tempo over USB, this app included, needs clock set to both.
Even with midi echo off, a universal identity request (SysEx) sent to the unit came back on its output; what forwards it is not known yet.
OS 1.0.15 fixed the echo setting being ignored for notes from linked tracks.
Start and stop received from one device are passed on to the other connected MIDI devices.
A monitor page in the same settings lists whatever MIDI arrives — channel, value, clock and SysEx — which tells a message that never arrived from one that arrived but was ignored.
Switches for what is sent to and received from each connected device live separately, under `com → M3` (devices).

steps.note: set its value (`turn E4` works too)

procedures.goal: Leave the system settings

parameters.name: section
parameters.note: system, keyboard, midi, clock, pitchbend, battery, monitor

units.body:
The midi section is where the OP-XY decides how it talks to other gear. Clock, notes and "other"
(every remaining message type, such as control changes) each get a direction, so the unit can, say,
take notes from a keyboard while ignoring its clock. The active track channel is a shortcut for playing
the OP-XY from a controller: whatever arrives on that channel plays the track you have selected.

Out of the box the unit only listens for clock (clock in), so it sends no start, stop or clock of
its own. Switching clock to both makes it a sync source: `play` and `stop` send start and stop, and
the tick stream runs continuously. This app suggests clock both during setup so it can follow the
unit's transport and tempo.

When a connection misbehaves, open the monitor page first: it shows whether a message reached the
OP-XY at all. Per-device switches live separately in `com → M3`.
